items.title: AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns
items.desc: METR reports that leading AI models like Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra are improving rapidly at research tasks but getting harder to measure. Current data can't rule out a dangerous acceleration in AI development, the organization warns, though it also says common tests may overestimate what the models can actually do. The article AI is getting better faster than experts can reliably test whether new systems are safe, METR warns appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: AI models are rapidly improving at AI research tasks, and they're getting harder to measure. According to the AI research organization METR , current public data isn't enough to rule out a drastic acceleration in AI research over the next few years. That could leave humans unable "to meaningfully understand, assess, and react to catastrophic risks posed by new AI systems," the organization warns. On clearly defined coding and computational tasks with direct feedback, the models already beat experienced human professionals most of the time, METR found, though they haven't yet outperformed large groups of top experts. For tasks that take humans longer, the task length the models can handle doubles every 3.6 months. A naive extrapolation of METR's data puts them at a 50 percent success rate on the longest, 200-hour tasks by July 2027. The systems still struggle with open-ended questions that lack immediate feedback and require real judgment, as well as with situations that are hard to recreate for training, according to METR. The organization also warns that common, easy-to-run tests may overestimate how well the models perform in real-world use, since developers train them in very similar test environments. items.title: Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct
items.desc: The Lean and Mathlib community has officially confirmed Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis as correct. Dozens of independent verifiers checked the 17 million lines of computer code. The solution arrived years earlier than expected: Terence Tao had predicted it wouldn't happen until around 2050 and didn't expect AI to solve it alone. The article Lean and Mathlib community officially confirms Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: The Lean and Mathlib community has confirmed that Levent Alpöge's proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct. "We have full confidence that Alpöge's proof is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement," the community said in a statement . Alpöge, a Stanford mathematician, published the proof on Nov. 20, 2026, as 17 million lines of code written in Lean , a tool that checks mathematical proofs for errors. Dozens of people ran the code independently and got the same result. The verification programs are designed so they provably cannot accept a flawed proof. MIT mathematician Andrew Sutherland lists the independent checks on his website . The Riemann hypothesis had been one of the most famous unsolved problems in math, making a prediction about how prime numbers are distributed. The video below, generated with Fable 5.2, explains the proof if you want to dig deeper. Ad The solution arrived much earlier than expected. As Ethan Mollick notes , forecasters on Metaculus had put the expected date at May 2035. Mathematician Terence Tao said last month he expected the problem to fall to "a combination of humans and AI around 2050 or so." Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website
items.desc: You can keep your WordPress site in good shape yet still lose leads to unanswered emails, missed follow-ups, and an out-of-date calendar. My Symphony review looks at a team of AI agents, led by one orchestrator, that can organize your work and wait for approval. The post " Symphony Review: A Team of AI Agents for the Business Behind Your Website " first appeared on WP Mayor .
items.full: To be a small business owner is to spin multiple plates at once: lead generation, client outreach, general marketing and sales, design, and much more. Often, some of those plates will fall and smash, which might mean you lose a good prospect, don’t hit a deadline, or myriad other negatives. By the end of this Symphony review, you might choose to take a breath and let its Maestro orchestrator organize your work tasks, so you can sweep up the broken crockery! Each of Symphony’s four pricing tiers comes with the core functionality of Maestro and the ability to use multiple AI agents around the clock. The difference between each plan is the number of AI credits you receive per month, the ‘activity level’ of your agents, the number of actions you have available, and your usage allocation. Here are the three premium plans: The cost I give here is based on annual billing. A month-by-month subscription costs slightly more. There aren’t any exact figures on the activity level of your agents and usage allocation either, just that higher tiers give you more. Free is more of an extended taster of what Symphony can give you. There’s an allocation of 500 credits per month and 100 daily credits. I think the Free plan is a generous offering given what’s included in the premium tiers. You also get two agent actions and briefings. If your credits run out before the month’s end, agents pause the work and wait for your credit allocation. It means you won’t need to adapt to an unfinished workflow or lose any work. If you run a small business, there are a few concerns you likely have regularly: This is what Symphony aims to improve. In a nutshell, you chat with Maestro (the orchestrator) and after it learns about your business, it dishes out the work to a set of AI agents. Each agent has one area of responsibility, but you can add custom agents if you need to work on a specific task. Wix claims the agent knowledge comes from 300 million businesses across a variety of regions and industries. Symphony is platform-agnostic , which means you don’t need to run a Wix site to use it (although you do need a Wix account). Instead, it connects to your calendars, email account, CRM, MCP server, and other tools. My first impression is that Symphony is going to be most helpful for single-person businesses or small teams. Freelancers or content creators fit the bill, but agencies that run several projects at once can also benefit. The Pro plan is likely the best fit for all of these business types. A freelancer with a small workload could opt for Basic, but you wouldn’t want to restrict your growth based on your Symphony plan. There are four core aspects to Symphony that cover the majority of your needs: Everything works through human-language prompts , and each project gets its own contained workspace. For instance, you can tell Maestro the details of your business and it assembles a team of AI agents based on the suitability for the task. It covers outreach and marketing, scheduling, research, design, and even finance. The information is also used to build a knowledge base, which involves a constant learning cycle. items.title: GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy
items.desc: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra independently produced a machine-verifiable Lean proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem, the first of its kind according to Vals AI. The model chose its own approach because key foundations were missing from Mathlib. On Autoform-Hard, Astra now leads the leaderboard with 49 of 56 tasks solved. The article GPT-6.2 Astra solved a math theorem no other AI could crack, then invented its own proof strategy appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: OpenAI's GPT-6.2 Astra produced a formalized, machine-verifiable proof of a 2006 theorem with zero human help during the run. According to Vals AI , it's the first known proof of Smoktunowicz's gap theorem written in Lean . The theorem states that when a mathematical system multiplies its basic building blocks, growth is either quite slow or very fast. There's no middle ground. Because key foundations of the original proof were missing from the math library Mathlib, Astra took a different route than the published mathematical proofs , Vals says. It used "capacity," a metric from existing research that checks the minimum number of elements added per computation step. This happened on Autoform-Hard , a subset of Meta FAIR's AutoformBench curated by Vals. It contains 56 tasks (five corrected) that ten models in Meta's study failed to solve within budget. When Astra tried to quit after 47 minutes and eight dollars, the system rejected the attempt since unsolved submissions aren't accepted until $20 has been spent. After nine minutes of silence with no code input while it searched for a new strategy, Astra delivered the 1,800-line proof at the 94-minute mark for $21.58. It now leads the leaderboard with 49 solved tasks, ahead of GPT-6.2 Sol and Claude Fable 5.2 at 48 each. Already a subscriber? Sign in

In this special episode of The WP Minute, Matt Medeiros sits down with Dan Maby, co-founder of Show.fm, to discuss the rapid changes happening across the WordPress ecosystem and what they mean for developers, agencies, and the wider community. Dan shares his perspective on the challenges facing WordPress events, the growing influence of AI, and the risks of building software without thinking about long-term maintenance, security, and sustainability. They also dig into the hidden costs of AI, the potential for vendor lock-in, and why being able to build something doesn’t always mean you should. Then, the conversation shifts to podcasting. Dan explains how he and Nathan Wrigley evolved Podcaster Plus into Show.fm, an end-to-end podcast operations platform designed to help creators manage everything from guest booking to publication. They explore guest discovery, automations, analytics, AI-powered research, and the importance of owning your content through RSS. Is WordPress at a crossroads? Is AI creating more work than it’s solving? And can podcasting become a more sustainable business? Let’s get into it. New articles and episodes, plus the week’s WordPress news. A five-minute read. items.title: Meta's Alexandr Wang warns the AI industry isn't ready for what's coming after Riemann breakthrough
items.desc: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The article Meta's Alexandr Wang warns the AI industry isn't ready for what's coming after Riemann breakthrough appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Meta's Chief AI Officer Alexandr Wang sees the recent AI-assisted proof sketch of the Riemann Hypothesis as a clear sign that superintelligence is right around the corner. The Riemann Hypothesis is widely considered the most intellectually demanding unsolved problem in mathematics. The brightest minds have failed to crack it for 150 years. The fact that an AI model played a major role in the breakthrough shows that raw intelligence is no longer the bottleneck, Wang argues. According to Wang, current models only lack domain-specific knowledge and practical infrastructure to outperform humans in nearly every field. That includes AI research itself. Since AI research is intellectually less demanding than the Riemann Hypothesis, Wang believes models could soon automate their own development and improve themselves. They could also dramatically speed up biological research, weapons research, and economic research at a pace humans can barely follow. Wang also warns that the AI industry isn't thinking hard enough about what comes next. In his view, many in the field treat superintelligence as inevitable and focus only on safety. But the stakes are much broader than that, he argues. The industry needs to actively ensure that AI gives people more agency rather than taking control of society. That would require a sharp departure from the current course, Wang says. Despite having its own superintelligence team , Meta isn't a major player at the frontier right now. items.title: Chinese military fears AI could let the US find and destroy its nuclear missiles
items.desc: Chinese military researchers fear that AI advances could give the US an edge in the nuclear balance of power. The article Chinese military fears AI could let the US find and destroy its nuclear missiles appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Chinese military researchers fear that AI advances could give the US an edge in the nuclear balance of power. Experts in China worry that artificial intelligence could make it easier for US forces to detect and destroy Chinese nuclear missiles, according to a New York Times analysis. That would undermine China's deterrence strategy, which relies on a guaranteed second-strike capability. Researchers at the Academy of Military Sciences in Beijing write that AI could shrink US decision-making time from 15 to 30 minutes down to 90 seconds. China currently has about 620 operational warheads, according to the Federation of American Scientists, and is expected to expand its arsenal to roughly 1,000 by 2030. At the same time, Chinese military institutes are studying how AI could make their own weapons harder to intercept, for instance by using AI-controlled flight paths for hypersonic missiles. Experts warn, however, that flawed AI data could trigger dangerous miscalculations during a crisis. That risk proved very real earlier this year, when the US military nearly boarded a Chinese ship based on a false, AI-generated intelligence report . Xi Jinping did discuss nuclear risks at a summit with Trump and Putin, but AI's role in nuclear weapons never came up, according to the report. Despite the growing urgency, the US and China have made almost no progress on talks about AI safeguards in nuclear systems. Ad Ad Already a subscriber? Sign in

items.title: Using Fallbacks for a Robust Front-End
items.desc: It’s important to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our users. Using Fallbacks for a Robust Front-End originally handwritten and published with love on CSS-Tricks . You should really get the newsletter as well.
items.full: NVIDIA L4 GPUs. 5-second cold starts. Scale to zero when idle. Anyone who has been working in web development for a while will be familiar with this now-legendary meme from xkcd . It illustrates just how fragile the technical infrastructure of a website or app can be. That’s why it’s important to use fallbacks to build a robust front end, either to quietly and discreetly avoid the error or to communicate it to our users. The issue of robustness is so important that it is actually one of the four principles of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (WCAG) ! So how can we provide a modern front end without excluding users who use browsers and hardware that are only partially compatible or not compatible at all? The answer lies in implementing multiple safety nets in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript, so that we are prepared for the worst-case scenario and can provide our users with the best possible experience. Two distinctions The main difference between the use of fallbacks and progressive enhancement lies in the directions in which the two approaches aim. While progressive enhancement is about automatically making certain features available as long as they are supported (forward), fallbacks are about what happens when something is not available or accessible (backward). For example, we can offer a shiny new CSS feature that makes interacting with our website even more enjoyable. But if this feature isn’t available in some browsers, no one will notice, because a version that’s supported by older browsers is available instead. Progressive enhancement in action! Another example: If JavaScript cannot be loaded for a critical application, we provide a fallback that either offers basic functionality or, at the very least, displays a message explaining what the problem is. While one doesn’t necessarily exclude the other, their approaches are quite different. My personal recommendation is to always work with progressive enhancement as a guiding principle and to consider fallbacks whenever possible. Web platform: Staying up-to-date with the web platform To evaluate new features intended for production, we must first determine the extent to which a feature is supported. Since 2023, the Interop project has been in place, in which major browser vendors collaborate to release new features for the web platform more or less simultaneously. This serves as a general overview. Related to this is the Baseline project, which shows, for specific features, the extent to which they are supported and how long they have been available. However, it is extremely important to note that it does not track browser support for accessibility features built into the web platform! Another important resource for checking compatibility is Can I Use . Here, you can get a quick overview of browser support for various features. HTML: Error pages and <noscript> Let’s start with the foundation of the World Wide Web: HTML. Modern tech stacks place a strong emphasis on client-side rendered JavaScript, which can offer many benefits to users in more complex applications. items.title: Anthropic's appetite for compute is pushing xAI toward a rent-over-build strategy
items.desc: Since May, SpaceXSI has been renting compute to competitors like Anthropic and Google while scaling back its own AI projects. Anthropic pays about $3.1 billion a month, Google $800 million, the New York Times reports. After its June IPO, SpaceXSI disbanded the 60-person Grok Imagine team, among other cuts. The article Anthropic's appetite for compute is pushing xAI toward a rent-over-build strategy appeared first on The Decoder .
items.full: Anthropic's massive compute needs align with growing profit pressure at xAI, Elon Musk's AI unit. xAI has rented compute to rivals since May, and its June IPO made the push for revenue even more urgent, the New York Times reports . Anthropic is now xAI's biggest customer with a contract worth roughly $3.1 billion a month. Google spends $800 million. Either deal can be canceled with 90 days' notice. xAI now accounts for over half of xAI's total revenue. Insiders say the company had to finish new data centers by October to fill Anthropic's orders, and Musk says the Claude maker wants to rent even more. In August, Musk pushed engineers in a group chat for "revenue per GPU," frustrated in part that xAI's own models can barely compete. He reportedly renamed an internal chat "Sell compute because we can't compete." Ad xAI is cutting or restructuring its own AI projects to match that shift. Unit chief Mike Nicolls told staff in November that the 60-person team behind the Grok Imagine image and video generator would be disbanded. An internal memo pointed to critical business priorities. xAI shut down its AI avatars in September, and OpenAI also killed its Sora video model over capacity limits. Ad Already a subscriber?
